# Verdict: `do_not_deploy`

This contract has multiple critical and high-severity issues that make it unsafe to deploy. Several are exploitable to drain funds or permanently brick the contract.

## Critical Issues

### 1. Unchecked `receive()` lets anyone buy without sending ETH meaningfully / break reserves — Lines 200-202
```solidity
receive() external payable {
    buy();
}
```
Because `buy()` is triggered on every plain ETH transfer, anyone sending ETH directly to the contract mints tokens to themselves at the contract's own spot price. Combined with the mispriced `getAmountOut` (see #3) and the fact that `buy()` ignores the swap fee logic used elsewhere, this is trivially abusable. Worse: during `sell()` and `removeLiquidity()` the contract does `payable(msg.sender).transfer(...)`, which can trigger `receive()` on the recipient if it's a contract — but more importantly, any external ETH push (e.g., selfdestruct) triggers `buy()` unexpectedly.

### 2. `sell()` transfers ETH **before** accounting for reentrancy and the ETH transfer itself changes reserves mid-call — Lines 183-198
```solidity
payable(msg.sender).transfer(ethAmount);
```
The ETH is sent as the last step, which is good, but the state has already been updated. However, `transfer` is 2300 gas, so classic reentrancy is limited. The real problem is elsewhere.

### 3. Reserve manipulation: `_balances[address(this)]` is the token reserve, but `buy()` can drain it in one tx — Lines 165-176
```solidity
uint256 token_amount = (swapValue * _balances[address(this)]) / (address(this).balance);
uint256 user_amount = token_amount * 50 / 100;
uint256 fee_amount = token_amount - user_amount;
_transfer(address(this), msg.sender, user_amount);
_transfer(address(this), feeReceiver, fee_amount);
```
On the very first buy, `_balances[address(this)]` is the entire supply and `address(this).balance` is the ETH added as liquidity. A buyer can sweep nearly all tokens in a single call. Combined with the code's intent that `getAmountOut` uses `((value * reserveToken) / (reserveETH + value)) / 2`, the actual `buy()` math is **inconsistent** with `getAmountOut()` and with `sell()` math. There is no `require` that reserves remain, so the pool can be emptied in one trade.

### 4. `sell()` will revert for most of the supply — Lines 187-196
```solidity
uint256 ethAmount = (sell_amount * address(this).balance) / (_balances[address(this)] + sell_amount);
...
_transfer(msg.sender, address(this), swap_amount);
_transfer(msg.sender, address(0), burn_amount);
```
`sell()` burns 50% of the sold tokens and sends 50% to the contract. The ETH payout is computed against `_balances[address(this)] + sell_amount`, but only `swap_amount` (half) is added to the reserve. The math under-counts the tokens added to the pool versus what the constant-product formula requires, slowly draining ETH faster than price-correct. Over time the pool becomes insolvent.

### 5. `removeLiquidity()` reads `address(this).balance` **after** sending it — Line 152
```solidity
payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance);
emit RemoveLiquidity(address(this).balance);
```
After `transfer`, `address(this).balance` is `0`, so the event always emits `0`. Cosmetic bug, but indicates sloppy test coverage.

### 6. Hardcoded owner and fee receiver — Lines 34-35
```solidity
address public feeReceiver = 0x93fBf6b2D322C6C3e7576814d6F0689e0A333e96;
address public owner = 0xCf309355E26636c77a22568F797deddcbE94e759;
```
The deployer is not the owner. Whoever controls those two hardcoded addresses has full control (`enableTrading`, `setFeeReceiver`, `renounceOwnership`, `transferOwnership`) and receives 50% of every buy. This is a backdoor/rug vector baked into the bytecode.

### 7. `unchecked` subtraction in `_transfer` can silently underflow — Lines 97-108
```solidity
unchecked {
  _balances[from] = _balances[from] - value;
}
```
The `require(_balances[from] >= value)` guard at line 95 makes the subtraction itself safe, but the `+=` to `_balances[to]` and the `-=` on `_totalSupply` are also unchecked. `_totalSupply -= value` when `to == address(0)` can underflow and wrap to a huge number if `value > _totalSupply` (only reachable if the balance check is bypassed via the burn path — here it is guarded, but the pattern is fragile and should not be unchecked).

### 8. Liquidity provider can `removeLiquidity` and brick all sells — Lines 146-154
Once liquidity is removed (allowed after the unlock block unconditionally), all outstanding holders' tokens are worthless — there's no ETH to sell into, and `tradingEnable = false` blocks all buys/sells. There is no minimum lock and no ownership of the LP position after `renounceLiquidityProvider()`. Combined with the fact that `liquidityProvider` is set by whoever calls `addLiquidity` first (line 141), an attacker can front-run to become the LP.

### 9. `addLiquidity` sets `blockToUnlockLiquidity` as an **absolute block number** — Lines 138-141
```solidity
require(block.number < _blockToUnlockLiquidity, 'Block number too low');
blockToUnlockLiquidity = _blockToUnlockLiquidity;
```
The parameter name implies a duration in the interface, but the implementation treats it as an absolute block. Callers who pass a small duration (e.g., `30`) will revert; callers who pass a huge value may lock funds forever. UX footgun and inconsistent with `extendLiquidityLock`'s semantics.

### 10. `tradingEnable` can only be flipped off via `removeLiquidity` — no pause path
If `tradingEnable` is true and the LP never calls `removeLiquidity`, there is no way to disable trading (no admin pause, no ownership check on `receive()`). Conversely, once set false by `removeLiquidity`, the only re-enable path is a fresh `addLiquidity`, but `liquidityAdded` is already `true`, so it permanently reverts. **Trading is dead forever after liquidity removal.**

### 11. First-buyer price manipulation on `addLiquidity`
`addLiquidity` sets `liquidityAdded = true` and enables trading, but does **not** verify that the contract's token balance is still intact. If anyone transferred tokens out of the contract (by sending ETH pre-addLiquidity — blocked because `tradingEnable=false` — but the owner can flip trading on *before* liquidity is added via `enableTrading(true)`), the pool can be initialized at a manipulated ratio.

### 12. `sell()` requires users to pre-approve nothing, but `transfer(to=this)` intercepts tokens meant for the contract
Line 88-92: any transfer to `address(this)` is interpreted as a sell. If a user intends to send tokens to the contract for any other reason, they'll instead trigger a sell and receive ETH. No way to distinguish.

## Summary of Issues (by line)

| Line | Severity | Issue |
|------|----------|-------|
| 34-35 | Critical | Hardcoded owner & feeReceiver backdoor |
| 88-92 | High | Any `transfer` to contract is a sell; no opt-out |
| 97-108 | Medium | Unchecked underflow on `_totalSupply` and `_balances[to]` |
| 138-141 | Medium | `_blockToUnlockLiquidity` treated as absolute block despite interface implying duration |
| 146-154 | High | LP can permanently brick trading; `liquidityAdded` never resets |
| 152 | Low | Event emits `0` after balance already sent |
| 160-168 | High | `buy()` math inconsistent with `getAmountOut`; can drain reserves |
| 165-176 | Critical | Single buy can sweep nearly the whole token reserve |
| 187-196 | High | `sell()` math slowly drains ETH; burns 50% of user tokens |
| 200-202 | Critical | `receive()` unconditionally calls `buy()` — anyone can self-mint |
| — | Critical | No slippage/deadline params; MEV sandwich is trivial |
| — | Medium | `getAmountOut` returns quote but is never used by `buy()`/`sell()` |

**Recommendation:** Do not deploy. The reserve math, the `receive()` auto-buy, the hardcoded owner/feeReceiver, and the permanent `tradingEnable=false` after LP removal are all disqualifying. Even after patching, this design (ERC-314 style) needs a full audit and invariants (x*y=k) enforced in both `buy` and `sell`.
